strengths: Identifies a subtle, critical mathematical inconsistency in FlashAttention's backward pass under QAT: the algebraic reduction $P_i^\top dP_i = dO_i^\top O_i$ breaks when $O_i$ is computed with quantized probabilities $P^F$ while $dP_i$ relies on the continuous chain rule. The proposed fix—accumulating an auxiliary high-precision output $O'_i$ during the forward pass—is mathematically sound and well-motivated.

Provides both Triton kernels (for training with inline PTX / bitwise emulation) and optimized CUDA kernels (for inference), running benchmarks on modern Blackwell-generation consumer hardware (RTX 5090).

Comprehensive empirical validation across two major domains: video diffusion (Wan 2.1 1.3B and 14B) and large language models (Qwen-3 14B, Llama 3.1 70B), demonstrating that QAT enables un-augmented FP4 attention to match BF16 quality while outperforming training-free methods like SageAttention3.
Eliminating runtime outlier-mitigation heuristics (e.g., QK smoothing and two-level quantization) leads to concrete end-to-end inference speedups (1.1x–1.5x) over SageAttention3.
Ablation studies clearly confirm the necessity of the proposed backward pass design: removing $O'$ causes exploding gradient norms, training collapse, and severe degradation in downstream evaluation.
weaknesses: Attn-QAT increases training memory overhead because it requires calculating and caching the high-precision forward tensor $O'$ and storing fake-quantized activation buffers, necessitating aggressive gradient checkpointing and sequence parallelism.
There are minor inconsistencies and typos in model descriptions: Appendix B.2 refers to continuing training on 'Qwen3-8B' while Section 3.1 and Table 4 refer to 'Qwen3-14B'.

On Llama 3.1 70B continued training (Table 4), Attn-QAT exhibits a visible performance gap compared to BF16 (e.g., WikiText perplexity of 0.3076 vs 0.2838; MMLU of 0.7773 vs 0.7881), which is attributed to computational budget constraints rather than systematically resolved.
Comparison against SageAttention3 is missing on the LLM benchmarks due to asserted kernel issues in SageAttention3's causal implementation, leaving the LLM comparisons limited to naive FP4 and BF16.

strengths: Insightful mathematical and architectural analysis: The paper pinpoints the exact failure modes when integrating QAT into tiled FlashAttention backward passes, specifically showing how the standard FlashAttention algebraic shortcut $P_i^\top dP_i = dO_i^\top O_i$ breaks when $O_i$ is computed with quantized probabilities $P^F$ while the softmax Jacobian uses unquantized $P$. Introducing an auxiliary high-precision output $O'$ neatly resolves this while preserving linear memory complexity.

Elimination of PTQ runtime heuristics: By training the model to adapt directly to standard NVFP4 representations, the method eliminates runtime Q/K smoothing and two-level quantization overheads required by PTQ approaches like SageAttention3, achieving a 1.1x–1.5x speedup on an RTX 5090.

Comprehensive empirical validation across modalities: The authors validate their method on both large-scale video diffusion models (Wan-2.1 1.3B and 14B) and LLMs (Qwen3-14B, Llama-3.1 70B), showing strong recovery of BF16 quality via continued training and direct supervised fine-tuning.
Thorough ablations: Table 2 and Figure 3 convincingly demonstrate the necessity of the proposed backward modifications, proving that omitting $O'$ leads to gradient explosion and unstable training.
weaknesses: Quantization scope restricted to attention: All linear layers (projections and FFNs) remain in BF16. In standard LLM decoding and moderate context lengths, linear layers typically dominate runtime and memory bandwidth, which constrains the end-to-end model speedup beyond isolated attention microbenchmarks.

Memory overhead during training: Computing and retaining the auxiliary high-precision output $O'$ adds memory pressure during the forward pass. As acknowledged in Appendix B.1, full gradient checkpointing and sequence parallelism were required to mitigate OOM errors; a quantitative memory profiling analysis comparing Attn-QAT against standard FlashAttention training would strengthen the paper.

Omission of FP4 PTQ baseline for LLMs: SageAttention3 is excluded from LLM experiments due to causal mask issues in its open-source kernel. While understandable, this leaves the LLM evaluation without an FP4 PTQ comparison to benchmark quality recovery against training-free alternatives.

Minor editorial inconsistency: Appendix B.2 refers to 'Qwen3-8B' in several places when describing continued training configurations, whereas the main text and Tables 3 and 4 report results for 'Qwen3-14B'.

strengths: Identifies and addresses a critical mathematical and architectural bottleneck: naively combining FP4 forward passes with FlashAttention-style backward passes breaks the key identity $P_i^\top dP_i = dO_i^\top O_i$. The proposed solution of computing and caching an auxiliary high-precision output $O'$ for backward gradient computation while keeping linear memory complexity is elegant and mathematically sound.
First systematic study successfully enabling quantization-aware training (QAT) for fused 4-bit attention, supported by custom Triton kernels for training and optimized CUDA kernels for FP4 inference.

Comprehensive evaluation across two major domains: video diffusion models (Wan-2.1 1.3B and 14B) and large language models (Qwen-14B and Llama-3.1 70B), validating both continued training and supervised fine-tuning.

Ablation studies convincingly show that QAT eliminates the need for complex, runtime-costly outlier mitigation heuristics (such as QK smoothing and two-level softmax quantization), yielding an end-to-end kernel speedup of 1.1x–1.5x over SageAttention3 on an RTX 5090 GPU.
weaknesses: Caching the extra high-precision tensor $O'$ increases training activation memory. While the paper mentions resorting to full activation checkpointing and Ulysses sequence parallelism to avoid out-of-memory errors (Appendix B.1), it lacks a systematic quantitative analysis/profiling of memory footprint and training speed overhead introduced by Attn-QAT compared to standard BF16 FlashAttention training.

In the LLM evaluations, SageAttention3 is omitted entirely due to reported implementation bugs in causal attention, leaving naive uncalibrated FP4 as the sole low-precision baseline for LLMs in Tables 3 and 4.
Minor inconsistencies in model names in Appendix B.2 (referencing 'Qwen3-8B' in the text of page 13, whereas Table 3 and Table 4 denote 'Qwen3-14B').

On video generation benchmarks (Table 1), while overall quality matches BF16, certain sub-metrics such as 'Dynamic Degree' show a noticeable drop from BF16 (0.5193 vs 0.3646), which warrants deeper discussion.
